value.statement: For every natural d, family of measurable spaces X_i indexed by i∈Fin(d+1), family of sigma-finite measures μ_i on X_i, and selected i∈Fin(d+1), the measurable equivalence e_i:(∏_k X_k)→X_i×(∏_{k∈Fin d}X_{i.succAbove(k)}) defined by e_i(x)=(x_i,(x_{i.succAbove(k)})_k) is measure preserving from the product measure ∏_k μ_k to μ_i×(∏_{k∈Fin d}μ_{i.succAbove(k)}). Here i.succAbove enumerates all the other indices in their order, and the inverse of e_i inserts the first coordinate at index i. Measure preserving means that the map is measurable and its pushforward measure is exactly the displayed target measure.

value.declaration: Define split(x)=(x_j,(x_k)_{k≠j}), with the remaining coordinates in increasing order; its inverse inserts the first coordinate at position j.

patches.value: For each fixed choice of the remaining n−1 coordinates in [−R,R], consider the scalar function of x_j obtained by restricting g to that coordinate line. It is smooth on ℝ, including both endpoints −R and R. Its derivative is continuous and hence integrable on this compact interval, and the function has zero value at both endpoints because these points lie on the boundary of Q, outside C. M002 therefore gives ∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g dx_j=0. To make the product identification explicit, define split(x)=(x_j,(x_k)_{k≠j}) with the other coordinates ordered increasingly. Insertion at position j is its inverse, as is checked coordinate by coordinate. Since 1≤j≤n, one has n=(n−1)+1. Apply M010 with d=n−1, every coordinate space ℝ, every coordinate measure the Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], and selected index j (converted to zero-based Fin n). Each coordinate measure is finite, hence sigma-finite. The source gives that split is a measure-preserving measurable equivalence between Lebesgue measure restricted to Q and the product of the jth restricted coordinate measure with the restricted product of the other coordinates; the original product of restrictions is the restriction of dx to Q because both agree on coordinate rectangles. Thus transport by split takes the integrable function ∂_{x_j}g on Q to its composition with insertion, with the same integral and integrability for this product measure. Now M003 integrates the selected first factor in the inner integral. The FTC equality just proved makes that inner integral zero at every choice of the remaining coordinates in their box. Hence ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=0. When n=1 the remaining coordinate space is a singleton with empty product measure of mass one, so the same argument reduces to the FTC equality. Endpoints do not affect the Lebesgue interval integral since singletons have zero measure.

value.bindings: A=ℝ for coordinate j, B_source=ℝ^(n−1) for the other ordered coordinates, μ=Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], ν=product of the other restricted coordinate measures, V=ℝ; f is ∂_{x_j}g composed with coordinate insertion.
hypothesis_checks: The coordinate measurable structures and real normed-space structures apply. Both factor measures are finite and therefore s-finite, since they are finite products of restricted measures of finite intervals.

F001 gives integrability of ∂_{x_j}g on Q, and M010 as applied in S002 transports this integrability under split to μ×ν. The source iterated integral has the selected jth coordinate as its inner integral.
